mechanism: IRIS decomposes world-model imagination into two coupled stages: (1) a discrete autoencoder (VQ-style encoder E + decoder D) compresses raw frames into sequences of discrete tokens — a learned symbolic vocabulary — and (2) an autoregressive Transformer G predicts the next token sequence, reward, and episode termination conditioned on the full history of token sequences and actions. The Transformer's global self-attention over this token history is what makes multi-step rollouts coherent; the policy is then trained entirely inside these imagined rollouts via actor-critic.
invariant: The bottleneck that makes imagination-based RL sample-efficient is world-model accuracy over long horizons. Compressing observations into discrete tokens and using a sequence model with global context (Transformer) keeps that accuracy high regardless of game, because the same mechanism — symbolic compression + causal attention — handles both spatial structure and temporal dependencies.
prediction: Replacing the Transformer backbone with a recurrent model of equal parameter count should degrade long-horizon rollout fidelity and downstream policy performance on Atari 100k, particularly on games requiring credit assignment over many steps — measurable as a drop in human-normalized score and in imagined-frame quality at step s > 10.

source_excerpt: IRIS, a data-efficient agent that learns in a world model composed of a discrete autoencoder and an autoregressive Transformer. [...] this framework relies heavily on accurate world models since the policy is purely trained in imagination. [...] designing new world model architectures, capable of handling visually complex and partially observable environments with few samples, is key to realize their potential as surrogate training grounds.
